An interactive Hebrew course (web app plus a companion book) with two goals: read Torah and prayers aloud with a
congregation, and get around in Israel without sounding like an outsider. It is a zero-dependency static PWA: plain ES
modules, no build step, served by any static file server. The course is called ALEF. This private repository is Al-Heb.
This project was inspired by Rabbi Bill Tepper (IJL class) and Rabbi Eliza McCaroll (Holy Blossom Temple).

Letter memory chain (draft).** Each of the 27 letter forms has a picture that turns into the letter, a sound hook word (for example loch, hut, cup, mailbox, swim ring, shortcake, feather, nuts) and one example word, with a short story written for each of the three pronunciation settings. It shows as a memory card on the letter page (above the tracing box until the letter has been traced), as review practice cards, a poster, flashcards and a book section. Of the 28 pictures, 9 are installed for offline use and 19 load on demand. The letters tests pass in a run on 2026-11-04 (223 tests, 222 pass, 1 skipped); no native speaker, teacher or learner has reviewed it, and its pictures are self-rated. Two shvas in a row mid-word: the first is silent, the second is vocal. Two at the end of a word: both silent.

Preview, written 2026-11-04. This is a plain account of what the builders measured. It is not a promise, not a legal document and not a conformance claim.
What this statement does not say
Aleph does not claim to meet WCAG, the ADA, EN 301 549 or any other standard or law. No outside accessibility audit has been done.
A check that found nothing means that check found nothing. It does not mean the screen works for you.

An automated checker (axe-core 4.14.0) was run in desktop Chromium over the screens of the app, at phone and desktop sizes, in light and dark colours (docs/A11Y.md). It finds only part of the problems a person can meet.

A walk using only the keyboard was done through six flows: first-run setup, tracing a letter, the letter atlas quiz, vocabulary review, the reader, and the calendar through the More menu (docs/A11Y.md). Known gaps are listed below.

Ten newer screens were measured by script for headings, names of buttons and fields, keyboard focus order and a visible focus ring, status messages, reduced motion, narrow-width layout (320 and 195 CSS pixels wide) and Hebrew language tagging (docs/a11y/NEWVIEWS.md).

Colour numbers: 112 text and component colour pairs for the light, dark and two high-contrast themes were computed from the CSS colours (docs/a11y/colourblind.md, tools/a11y/contrast.mjs). All meet their target (4.5 to 1 for text, 3 to 1 for components) except one yellow picture fill, which is 1.31 to 1.

Right and wrong answers: where colour was the only sign in some answer screens, a tick or cross and words were added. Screens were looked at through simulated colour-blindness filters by the builder, and some screens were checked only by reading the code (docs/a11y/colourblind.md).

Hearing: the places in the code that play, record or listen to sound were listed, and the "I do not use audio" setting hides the Listen button on many of them and replaces listening-only questions with reading ones. Tests run the code paths (docs/a11y/deaf-hoh.md).

Calm mode and reading comfort (text size, spacing, line length, font): tested by unit tests on a fake DOM and by one desktop Chromium run that read computed styles. The code was searched for animation and flashing, and nothing was found that changes more than 3 times per second; this was a code read, not a measurement with a flash analyser (docs/a11y/COGNITIVE.md).

Plain wording: 21 strings the builder judged long were rewritten; the average sentence went from 11.1 to 7.5 words by a word-counting script. Those strings were chosen by the builder, so this is not a measure of the whole app (docs/a11y/COGNITIVE.md).

Movement and touch: a Tab-key walk of 23 screens in desktop Chromium found no keyboard trap, every visible control reachable, a visible focus mark on each stop and no jumps back up the page (144 checks). Tap targets were measured by script at an emulated phone size of 375 by 667: none of 908 targets on 32 screens is under 44 by 44 CSS pixels. Letters, Atlas and the quick checks need no dragging or sliding gestures; stroke tracing has a stroke-by-stroke button mode that is recorded as walked through, not as drawn. Time limits, automatic advance, undo and one-handed placement are covered in docs/a11y/motor.md.
The settings on the Accessibility screen exist, are checked when saved, are kept on this device and are included in a backup. This was tested in code (tests/a11y.hub.test.js).
What was not tested with real people or devices
No screen reader (VoiceOver, TalkBack, NVDA, JAWS) was used, so how the screens sound is unknown. No braille display, voice control or switch access was used.

No switch device, eye tracker, head pointer or voice-control software was used, and no person with a motor disability tried the app. Target sizes are CSS pixels in an emulator, not measured on a finger.
No real phone or tablet (iOS or Android) and no physical keyboard was used; checks ran in desktop Chromium, some at an emulated phone size.

Nobody with dyslexia, ADHD, memory difficulties, anxiety, sensory sensitivity, migraine or low literacy tried the calm mode, short sessions or reading settings, and no photosensitivity analyser was used.

No person with a disability, and no person who is deaf, blind, colour-blind, has limited movement or finds screens overwhelming, tried the app for this statement. Whether a setting helps a given person is not known.
Pinch zoom was not tested; narrow-width layout was used as a stand-in.
Hebrew labels in the interface were not proofread by a Hebrew speaker.

docs/A11Y.md lists open items from its 2026-11-04 run. Some have been worked on since (for example letter tracing now has a stroke-by-stroke button mode, and the letter atlas keeps keyboard focus), but only the automated keyboard walk in desktop Chromium has re-checked them, not a person using a keyboard or switch.

The 44 pixel measurement covers 32 screens at one phone size, not every screen. The "Size of buttons and fields: Large" setting was measured on the same screens: all but 49 targets reach 60 pixels (the on-screen typing keys are 56 wide, one paste box is 54 tall, one link is 48). Only lesson quick checks have "Ask me to confirm each answer"; "Keep the main buttons at the bottom" covers Review, first 10 minutes and Word Sprint; the single-key shortcuts setting does not reach the vocabulary list, Torah reader or typing trainer (docs/a11y/motor.md).

The default border around cards and fields is only about 1.4 to 1 against the page, below the 3 to 1 target for field edges. The two high-contrast themes make the edges solid (docs/a11y/colourblind.md).

"I do not use audio" does not yet hide every optional play button (for example on the letter atlas, Torah reader, vocabulary and scan screens), and first-run setup does not ask about it; the written text is shown next to those buttons (docs/a11y/deaf-hoh.md).
Written descriptions of sounds are drafts that no Hebrew speaker has checked, and words cannot replace hearing a sound (docs/a11y/deaf-hoh.md).

Calm mode removes the Torah "read with me" timer (Previous word and Next word stay, so you move the highlight by hand), but does not change the letter-tracing layout or the letter atlas, which still show a lot at once. Pause and resume covers the lesson page and its quick check, not every practice screen (docs/a11y/COGNITIVE.md).

3. What the research says, and how Aleph uses it

These are findings reported in the research notes for this project (study summaries read on 2026-11-03). Where the notes only had a blog or abstract summary, that is stated. They describe other learners in other settings. Aleph has not measured any learning outcome of its own.
Latimier, Peyre and Ramus (2021), 29 studies: spaced retrieval practice beat massed retrieval practice (g = 0.74). Expanding and uniform schedules did not differ (g = 0.034).

Cepeda et al. (2008), 1,354 participants: the best gap between study and review grows with how long you want to remember, but as a shrinking fraction (about 20-40% of a one-week interval, 5-10% of a one-year interval). Optimal spacing gave a 64% recall gain over massed study at equal study time, and gaps that were too short cost more than gaps that were too long.
Retrieval practice beat restudy across 217 studies (Adesope, Trevisan and Sundararajan, 2017; the notes only had a blog summary, without effect sizes).

every review card makes you recall first ("Show answer" comes after you try), and the scheduler spaces the next review by how well you remembered. The scheduler is FSRS-style and written from scratch for Aleph. It is not the reference FSRS implementation, does not use FSRS's published weights, and its constants have not been fitted to review data. (In an open benchmark of 349.9 million reviews, FSRS-6 had lower log loss than SM-2 for 99.6% of users, with the caveat that SM-2 was not built to output probabilities. That result is about FSRS, not about Aleph's version.)

Brunmair and Richter (2019), 59 studies: interleaved practice beat blocked practice overall (g = 0.42), most strongly for visual material (g = 0.67) and when categories are similar to each other. For word learning, blocking was better (g = -0.39).

new words and letters are taught in blocks inside a lesson, but in review, letters that look alike (for example bet and kaf, dalet and resh) are placed next to each other instead of being drilled in separate blocks. The sets are in data/letters/confusables.json.

Manalo, Mizutani and Trafford (2004) tested picture mnemonics for Japanese kana: pass rate rose from 51% to 65%, in a self-selected group of 27 with no effect size or retention data; the authors call it preliminary.

Shmidman and Ehri (2010), per a literacy blog and a reader comment in the notes (the paper itself was not read): English-speaking preschoolers learning ten Hebrew letters learned faster and made fewer errors with embedded picture mnemonics, where the letter shape is drawn into the picture. The same sources caution that pictures can hurt whole-word learning and that the evidence base is thin.

mnemonic pictures are planned as a temporary scaffold to fade, with letters that have two sounds (bet, kaf, pe, shin) handled with two states. No finished mnemonic artwork is in the app yet: the images are placeholders.

Shepperd (2024), a review: for beginners, input in an unfamiliar script gave little benefit for learning new sound contrasts compared with audio only, and sometimes hurt; the benefit grows with proficiency. Most of the studies were small, single-session samples of English speakers.
letters and vowels are paired with audio from the first lesson, and the hard sounds (resh, chet, ayin) are meant to be learned by listening and explicit instruction, not from the written shape alone.

A meta-analysis (Ngo, Chen and Lai) found explicit corrective feedback from speech recognition worked better than indirect feedback (g = 0.86 vs 0.50). Aleph has no speech-recognition feedback: you cannot yet speak to it and be scored. Handwriting tracing exists but its stroke data is a draft.

5. Privacy: your data stays on your device
Settings, completed lessons, review cards and your streak are stored in your browser's local storage on this device. There is no account, no server-side profile and no analytics in this build.
The app's own requests go only to the site that serves it (pages, fonts, data files, audio files when they exist).
Location is optional, used only to compute candle-lighting times on your device, and you can clear it in Settings.
Photo scan: recognition runs on this device with tesseract.js; no photo is uploaded.

Your progress, settings, review cards and streaks are saved in your browser, on this device (see the table below). There is no account, and no profile is kept on a server.
Reading text from a photo happens in your browser. The first time, it downloads about 5 MB of reading data from the Aleph site and keeps it for later.

Spoken audio uses your browser's built-in speech voice, or a short synthetic clip that is one of Aleph's own files. Aleph sends no text to any server for this. Which voice is used, and whether a particular voice runs on your device or online, is decided by your browser and device, and Aleph cannot tell which.

Record and compare asks your browser for microphone permission only when you press Record. The recording is kept in the page's memory as a temporary in-browser file so you can play it back. Aleph does not save it to storage, does not upload it and does not send it anywhere; it is dropped when you press Next or leave the screen. Only counts of your "heard a difference" answers are saved. On the hosted site the Permissions-Policy header in _headers sets microphone=(self), so a browser following it allows the microphone for Aleph's own address only and no embedded or third-party content; this was read in the file, not tested live.
Your gender setting for Hebrew forms (optional) and your word-roots, vowel-fade and gender-drill counts are saved in the settings and keys listed below. They are used on your device only.

Your location is read only when you press the button in Settings. The latitude and longitude are saved in your settings and used on your device for candle-lighting times. Nothing in the code sends them anywhere. You can type numbers instead, or clear them.

Reminders: the app shows notifications while it is open or via the service worker only after you allow them. No push server is configured (the push key is empty in src/shell/notify.js), so nothing is pushed to you from a server.
Calendar and progress files are made in your browser and handed to you as downloads. The Teacher screen can copy a code to your clipboard when you press its button.

A service worker (sw.js) keeps an offline copy of the app in the browser's Cache Storage, in caches named alef-shell-<version>, alef-data-<version> and alef-runtime-v1 (audio clips). They hold Aleph's own files only.

On the Scan screen, "Take or choose a photo" is the browser's own file picker, which on a phone can open the camera. Aleph itself never calls the camera API and reads the chosen photo in your browser. The Permissions-Policy header in _headers also allows camera=(self); read in the file, not tested on a device.

This is a plain summary of what this version of Aleph does with your data. It was written by reading the app's code. It is not legal advice. If you were given a different version, ask the person who gave it to you.

Short version: Aleph has no account, no analytics and no advertising code (searched for in the source). By default your progress stays in your browser. One optional feature can send something off your device and is described below: your browser's own speech recognition on the Say it screen. Online vowel points are not offered on the Scan screen in this build.
… of the … kinds of network request below can carry something you typed, scanned or said. Everything else only fetches Aleph's own files.
What was searched for and not found

The source was searched for analytics or tracking libraries, cookies, beacons, push subscriptions with a live key, camera or microphone uploads by Aleph itself, and any request that sends progress or settings anywhere. None was found in this build. The Vision OCR adapter in src/photo/engines/web.js exists as code but nothing in the app creates it. This is a code reading, not a network capture on a live site.
Your browser, your device vendor and the site's host can still log ordinary things such as your IP address when the app loads. Aleph cannot see or control that.
What is stored in your browser

Stored in localStorage on this device (one row, the scroll position, uses sessionStorage as it says). Each key below is saved with the prefix "alef:", except the three rows that say they use an exact name. Aleph uses no IndexedDB and no cookies; the only other place it keeps data is the browser's Cache Storage, which holds copies of Aleph's own files (and audio files, if any) and no progress or settings. If localStorage is unavailable (for example private browsing), the app keeps this data in memory only and it is lost when you close the tab. Review cards, progress and settings contain what you did in the app, not your name or account.
Settings > Backup > "Download backup" saves every alef: key as one JSON file. The Progress screen can also save a progress-only file.

Settings has a "Delete all my data" button. You type DELETE to confirm. It removes your progress, review cards, streaks and settings from this device, and it can also remove the offline copy of the app. You can also clear this site's data in your browser settings, or uninstall the app if you installed it. The same letter: with a dagesh dot it is b, without it is v. Real in every tradition, so a browser voice can carry it.

In Israeli Hebrew, and in the browser voice, het and khaf sound the same (a throaty kh), so this is a spelling check, not a listening one. Mizrahi, Yemenite and some Sephardi speakers pronounce het deeper in the throat; only a recording in such a voice would make it a true listening drill.

Is the vowel after the marked letter a or o?

Kamatz is usually a, but kamatz katan is o and looks the same in print. Ashkenazi reading says o for every kamatz. The browser voice may read a kamatz katan as a: only a recorded clip can be trusted for those words.
sh as in "ship" (dot on the right)

Same letter, two sounds, told apart by which side the dot sits on. Real in every tradition.

From general knowledge, not tested here.

Switch keyboards with the Windows key + Space (or Left Alt + Shift).

Type the letter first, then the mark: the mark attaches to the letter before it.
System Settings, Keyboard, Input Sources: add a Hebrew layout (more than one Hebrew layout may be offered).
Switch with the Input menu in the menu bar, or Control + Space.

To find vowel points on your layout, turn on Show Keyboard Viewer from the Input menu and hold the Option key (and Shift + Option): the points, if the layout has them, show on the keys. The key positions differ between layouts, so the table below may not match.
Type the letter first, then the mark.
Settings, General, Keyboard, Keyboards, Add New Keyboard: choose Hebrew.
Tap the globe key to switch keyboards.

Type the letter first, then the mark.
In your keyboard app (for example Gboard), open its settings, Languages, add keyboard: choose Hebrew.
Tap the globe key (or touch and hold the space bar) to switch.

Type the letter first, then the mark.

Shin and sin: type shin (ש), then the right dot (shin dot) or left dot (sin dot).

Explanatory copy for the day pages (/day/<iso-date>). Written for Aleph 2026-11-07 in plain English, Reform-friendly, no halachic ruling: dates and customs are the widely shared ones; a community's own practice comes first. Keys are the holiday ids of src/curriculum/calendar.js plus the generic days (shabbat, erev-shabbat, rosh-chodesh, erev-festival). `tr` follows the app's transliteration style (data/homepage/prayers.json: Israeli reading, ch for chet and chaf, no diacritics). `words` carry pointed Hebrew written for this file; not reviewed by a Hebrew teacher. `readings` name what is read or said; `texts` are ids of data/corpus/registry.json that the app can open (shown only when the id exists in the loaded registry). `lesson` is the festival word pack id under /festivals/<id> (shown only when the route exists). Nothing here renders audio.
Shabbat is the weekly day of rest, from Friday at sundown to Saturday after nightfall.
It recalls the seventh day of creation (Genesis 2:1-3) and the going out from Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15), and the Ten Commandments ask us to remember it and keep it.
For most Jews it is the centre of the week: candles, a shared meal, a slower pace, prayer and the weekly Torah portion.
Reform Judaism treats how to rest as a personal and family choice; the invitation is to set the day apart in a way that is meaningful to you.
Friday evening: light two candles before sunset, say Kiddush over wine or grape juice and HaMotzi over two challot.
Kabbalat Shabbat (welcoming Shabbat) in the synagogue, with the song Lecha Dodi.
Saturday morning: the weekly Torah portion and its haftarah are read.
Saturday night: Havdalah with wine, spices and a braided candle marks the return to the week.
separation; the ceremony that ends Shabbat
Candle blessing, Kiddush and HaMotzi on Friday evening
The weekly Torah portion and haftarah on Saturday morning
The Jewish day begins at sundown, so Shabbat starts on Friday evening.
Friday is the day of getting ready: cooking, setting the table, and lighting candles before sunset.
The candle-lighting time shown on this page is a fixed number of minutes before sunset for your chosen city, the custom most communities follow.
Light the candles before the time shown, then say the blessing.
Kiddush over wine or grape juice, HaMotzi over challah, and a shared meal.
evening; the eve of a day
Rosh Chodesh, literally 'head of the month', marks the start of each month of the Hebrew calendar, which follows the moon.
A Hebrew month has 29 or 30 days; after a 30-day month Rosh Chodesh lasts two days (the 30th and the 1st).
In the Torah it was announced with trumpet blasts and extra offerings (Numbers 10:10, 28:11-15); today it is a small festive day with additions to the prayers.
It has long been linked with women, and many Reform and other communities hold women's Rosh Chodesh groups.
Half-Hallel (psalms of praise) and Ya'aleh V'yavo are added to the service; the Torah reading is Numbers 28:1-15.
The new month is announced in the synagogue on the Shabbat before (Birkat HaChodesh).
People wish each other 'chodesh tov', a good month.
A festival begins at sundown the evening before its date, so this evening is when the holiday starts.
On the eve of a major festival candles are lit before sunset, as on Friday, with the festival's blessing and Shehecheyanu.
Light candles before the time shown.
A festive meal with Kiddush for the festival.
Rosh Hashanah, on 1 Tishrei, is the Jewish New Year and the start of the ten Days of Awe that end on Yom Kippur.
The Torah calls it a day of sounding the shofar (Numbers 29:1); the rabbis understood it as the anniversary of creation and a day of judgement, when the world and each life are weighed.
Its mood is serious but hopeful: honest self-examination, apology and repair, together with sweet food for a sweet year.
Most North American Reform congregations keep one day; some keep two, as Israel and traditional communities do.
Hearing the shofar, a ram's horn, blown in the synagogue.
Apples dipped in honey and a round challah, for a sweet, whole year.
Tashlich: casting breadcrumbs into flowing water on the afternoon of the first day, symbolically letting go of the past year's wrongs.
Greeting: Shanah tovah, a good year, or L'shanah tovah tikateivu, may you be written for a good year.
Torah: the binding of Isaac, Genesis 22 (read on the first day in most Reform congregations) and Genesis 21
Haftarah: 1 Samuel 1-2:10, and Jeremiah 31 on the second day
The shofar service: Malchuyot, Zichronot, Shofarot
Yom Kippur, on 10 Tishrei, is the holiest day of the Jewish year, a day of fasting, prayer and atonement that closes the Days of Awe.
The Torah sets it as a day to 'afflict yourselves' and do no work (Leviticus 16:29-31, 23:27-32).
Tradition teaches that it atones for wrongs between a person and God, but wrongs against other people must first be put right with them.
It is one day in every stream of Judaism, from sundown to nightfall, about 25 hours.
Fasting from food and drink (those whose health does not allow it are not expected to fast).
Wearing white; many avoid leather shoes.
Five services, from Kol Nidrei in the evening to Ne'ilah at dusk, ending with one long shofar blast.
Confession (Vidui) said together in the plural, and Yizkor, the memorial prayer.
Greeting: G'mar chatimah tovah, may you be sealed for good.
'all vows', the evening prayer that opens the day
may you be sealed for good (the greeting)
Torah: Deuteronomy 29:9-14 and 30:11-20 in Reform congregations (Leviticus 16 in traditional ones); Haftarah Isaiah 57:14-58:14
Afternoon: Leviticus 19 (Reform) and the Book of Jonah
Sukkot begins on 15 Tishrei, five days after Yom Kippur, and lasts seven days; the first day is a full festival day and the rest are Chol HaMoed, the festival's weekdays.
It recalls the forty years in the wilderness, when the Israelites lived in temporary shelters (Leviticus 23:42-43), and it is the autumn harvest festival, called 'the season of our joy'.
The sukkah, a hut with a roof of branches open to the sky, is a reminder of how fragile shelter is and how much we depend on one another.
It is one of the three pilgrimage festivals, with Pesach and Shavuot.
Building a sukkah and eating, and sometimes sleeping, in it.
Waving the four species: lulav (palm), hadas (myrtle), aravah (willow) and etrog (citron).
Inviting guests, including the symbolic ushpizin, the ancestors.
Hallel and the festival Kiddush; Shehecheyanu on the first night.
Torah: Leviticus 22:26-23:44 on the first day
Hallel each day; Kohelet (Ecclesiastes) on the Shabbat of Chol HaMoed
Shemini Atzeret, the 'eighth day of assembly' on 22 Tishrei, closes the Sukkot season as a festival of its own (Leviticus 23:36).
Simchat Torah, 'rejoicing in the Torah', is the day the yearly cycle of Torah reading ends and begins again: the last verses of Deuteronomy are read and then the first verses of Genesis.
In Israel and in Reform congregations the two are kept on the same day; traditional diaspora communities keep Simchat Torah on the next day, 23 Tishrei.
The prayer for rain (Geshem) is said from this day, as the rainy season begins in the Land of Israel.
Hakafot: carrying the Torah scrolls around the synagogue in seven circuits, with singing and dancing.
Every scroll is taken out; children are called up together for a blessing under a tallit.
Reading the end of Deuteronomy (V'zot HaBerachah) and the beginning of Genesis.
Yizkor is said on Shemini Atzeret.
'In the beginning', the first word of the Torah
V'zot HaTorah as each scroll is lifted
Simchat Torah, 'rejoicing in the Torah', is the day the yearly cycle of Torah reading ends and begins again.
The last verses of Deuteronomy are read and then, without a pause, the first verses of Genesis: the Torah has no end.
In traditional diaspora communities it falls on 23 Tishrei, the day after Shemini Atzeret; in Israel and in Reform congregations the two are one day.
Hakafot: seven circuits around the synagogue with every Torah scroll, singing and dancing.
Children are called up together for a blessing under a tallit.
Hanukkah begins on 25 Kislev and lasts eight nights.
It recalls the Maccabees' victory over the Seleucid Greek empire in 164 BCE and the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem; 'Chanukah' means dedication.
The Talmud tells of one day's oil that burned for eight days, and the eight lights also stand for the right to live and worship as Jews.
It is a minor festival (work is allowed) with a large place in family life: lights, songs, games and fried food.
Lighting the chanukiyah each night after dark: one candle the first night, adding one each night, lit from the shamash, the helper candle; the lights are placed where they can be seen.
Two blessings each night, and Shehecheyanu on the first night; Hanerot Halalu and Maoz Tzur are sung.
Foods fried in oil: latkes (levivot) and jam doughnuts (sufganiyot).
Spinning the dreidel (sevivon) and giving gelt or small gifts.
Blessings for lighting the candles; Shehecheyanu on the first night
Al HaNissim added to the Amidah and to Birkat Hamazon; full Hallel each morning
Torah: the dedication gifts of the princes, Numbers 7; Haftarah Zechariah 2:14-4:7 on Shabbat Hanukkah
Tu BiShvat (the New Year for Trees)
Tu BiShvat is the 15th of Shevat; the name is the date itself, since the letters tet and vav add up to fifteen.
The Mishnah names it the new year for trees, the date from which a tree's age was counted for tithes.
The mystics of sixteenth-century Safed gave it a seder of fruits and wine, and in modern Israel it became a day of planting trees.
Many Reform communities keep it as a Jewish Earth Day, a time to think about the natural world and our care for it.
Eating fruit, especially the seven species of the Land of Israel: wheat, barley, grapes, figs, pomegranates, olives and dates.
A Tu BiShvat seder with four cups of wine from white to red.
Planting trees, or giving towards planting.
No special Torah reading; a Tu BiShvat seder is a home or community custom
Blessings over fruit and over wine
Shehecheyanu over a fruit not yet eaten this season
Purim, on 14 Adar (Adar II in a leap year), celebrates the rescue of the Jews of Persia told in the Book of Esther.
Haman, the king's minister, plotted to destroy them; Queen Esther, with her cousin Mordechai, risked her life to reveal the plot, and the day meant for destruction became a day of joy.
The name comes from the lots (purim) Haman cast to choose the date.
It is a minor festival with the loudest, most playful mood of the year, and a serious core: gifts to the poor are one of its four duties.
Hearing the Megillah (the Book of Esther) read in the evening and again in the morning, drowning out Haman's name with noisemakers.
Mishlo'ach manot: sending gifts of food to friends; matanot la'evyonim: gifts to the poor.
A festive meal (se'udah), costumes, Purim plays (shpiels) and hamantaschen, the triangular filled pastries.
Megillat Esther, evening and morning, with its blessings
Al HaNissim added to the Amidah and Birkat Hamazon
Pesach begins on 15 Nisan and lasts seven days (eight in traditional diaspora practice); the first and last days are full festival days.
It celebrates the Exodus, the going out of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, and the Torah asks every generation to tell the story as if we ourselves had gone out.
Its name recalls the night God 'passed over' the Israelite houses (Exodus 12), and the matzah recalls bread that had no time to rise.
It is the spring festival and the first of the three pilgrimage festivals, and the counting of the Omer towards Shavuot begins on its second night.

The seder on the first night (many homes hold one on the second night too): the Haggadah, four cups of wine, four questions, matzah, maror (bitter herbs), charoset, the seder plate and the hidden afikoman.
Eating no chametz (leavened grain) for the whole festival; cleaning the home beforehand.
Hallel; Shir HaShirim (the Song of Songs) on the Shabbat of Chol HaMoed; Yizkor on the last day.
Torah: Exodus 12:21-51 on the first day; the Song of the Sea, Exodus 13:17-15:26, on the seventh day
Haftarah: Joshua 5:2-6:1 on the first day
Kiddush, Shehecheyanu and the Haggadah at the seder; Hallel
Yom HaShoah, on 27 Nisan, is the day of remembrance for the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust and for the Jewish resistance, set by Israel's Knesset in 1951.
The date falls between the anniversary of the Warsaw Ghetto uprising and Yom HaAtzmaut; it is moved a day if it would fall on Friday or Sunday.
In Israel a two-minute siren at 10:00 brings the country to a standstill.
Jewish communities everywhere hold memorial gatherings; there is no fixed liturgy, and many Reform congregations use readings, survivor testimony and the memorial prayers.
Lighting six candles, one for each million.
Reading names of the murdered; survivor and second-generation testimony.
El Malei Rachamim and the Mourner's Kaddish.
Memorial service: El Malei Rachamim, Mourner's Kaddish
Readings and testimony chosen by the community
Yom HaZikaron, on 4 Iyar, is Israel's day of remembrance for fallen soldiers and for victims of terror.
It is set the day before Yom HaAtzmaut, so that independence is celebrated with its cost in mind; both days shift when they would fall next to Shabbat.
Sirens sound across Israel at 20:00 as the day begins and at 11:00 the next morning; traffic stops and people stand in silence.
Communities outside Israel mark it with memorial ceremonies, often together with Yom HaAtzmaut.
Standing in silence for the sirens.
Memorial ceremonies at military cemeteries and in schools and synagogues; Yizkor and the Mourner's Kaddish.
At nightfall a ceremony on Mount Herzl marks the passage into Yom HaAtzmaut.
Yom HaAtzmaut, on 5 Iyar, celebrates the declaration of the State of Israel on 14 May 1948.
It is moved to Thursday if it would fall on Friday or Saturday, and to Tuesday if it would fall on Monday, so that it does not run into Shabbat.
It begins the moment Yom HaZikaron ends, at nightfall, with a torch-lighting ceremony on Mount Herzl.
Many Reform and other congregations treat it as a religious as well as a national day and add Hallel and a prayer for the State of Israel.
Fireworks, concerts and the national anthem, Hatikvah; flags on balconies and cars.

Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, is the saddest day of the Jewish year, a full fast from sundown to nightfall.

It mourns the destruction of the First Temple by Babylon in 586 BCE and of the Second Temple by Rome in 70 CE, and tradition attaches other catastrophes to the date, including the expulsion from Spain in 1492.
When 9 Av falls on Shabbat the fast is moved to Sunday, 10 Av.
Reform observance varies: many communities keep the fast and the reading of Lamentations, others mark the day with study of Jewish history and loss, and some do not observe it.
Fasting; sitting on low stools or the floor; dim lights.
Reading Eichah (Lamentations) in the evening, chanted to its own mournful melody, and kinot (laments).
No tallit or tefillin in the morning service, worn instead in the afternoon.
The three weeks before are a period of lessening joy; the Shabbat after is Shabbat Nachamu, of comfort.

These two letters look alike. Find the one feature that differs, then say the name before you pick.
Bet has a flat base that sticks out to the right; kaf is one smooth curve with no corner. Check the base first.
A vowel sign is a tiny mark under or beside the letter. Look at its shape and its place before you guess.
Two dots side by side under a letter (tzere) say 'e' as in bed ('ay' in Ashkenazi); two dots stacked (shva) are a very short sound or silent.
Hebrew reads right to left. Start at the right edge of the word and move left, letter by letter.
In שָׁלוֹם start at ש (sh), then ל (l), then ו (o), end at ם (m): sha-lom.
Aleph and ayin carry a vowel but add no consonant sound of their own in everyday Israeli speech.
In אַבָּא only the vowels are heard: a-ba. The first alef just holds the 'a' vowel.
Five letters change shape at the end of a word. The sound stays the same; only the shape changes.
כ at the start of a word and ך at the end are both kaf: the final one has a long tail down.
Everyday Hebrew text leaves most vowels out. In this course the marks are shown: read each one in order.
Without marks שלום is just ש-ל-ו-ם; with marks שָׁלוֹם you can read sha-lom.

The word for "the": ha- and the doubled letter
Hebrew has one word for "the", a small prefix glued to the front of a noun.

Hebrew has no separate word for the. It is a prefix, ha-, joined to the front of the noun, and it never changes for gender or number. The ha- is usually pointed with a patach, and the first letter of the noun then takes a dagesh, a dot that doubles the sound. So the dot is a trace of the doubling, not a new sound you must pronounce loudly. A few letters cannot take a dagesh: the guttural letters aleph, ayin and resh, and usually also he and chet. Before those letters ha- stretches to ha with a long a, or sometimes a short vowel, to make up for the missing doubling. That is why one prayer word has a long a after the h and another has a short one. Spot the pattern in the examples below, then try to match each form to its meaning. Remember that the article goes on the noun, and an adjective that follows takes its own copy.
One-letter prefixes: ve-, be-, le-, me-, she-
Small words such as and, in, to, from and that are written as one letter stuck to the next word.

Several very small words are not written alone. They are single letters attached to the front of the next word: ve- means and, be- means in or with, le- means to or for, me- means from, and she- means that or which. Most of them are pointed with a short sheva, which is a very quick vowel, so ve-, be- and le- sound like one light syllable before the word. The letter me- usually has a hiriq and sounds like mi. The prefix she- has a segol. These prefixes change little: the word they join keeps its own form, which makes them easy to spot once you know the five letters. In the examples the prefix is split off so you can see what is left. Be careful, since a few words simply begin with one of these letters without being prefixed. The rule here only claims a prefix when the leftover word is a listed word.
Two nouns side by side can mean "X of Y" without a separate word for of.

Hebrew often says X of Y by putting two nouns side by side. There is no word for of. This is called the construct state, or smichut. The first noun, the one that owns or describes, often shortens or changes its ending, and it can never take the word for the. Only the second noun can carry it, and then the whole chain counts as definite. A plural first noun often ends in an -ei sound instead of -im. So a tree of life is simply tree, life, and children of Israel is children, Israel. A dash called a maqaf sometimes ties the pair into a single written word. In the examples below, the chains come straight from prayer and Torah lines. The English meaning is written beside each one. Read the English first, then find the two Hebrew words that make the chain.

text: Most masculine nouns take -im and most feminine nouns take -ot, with exceptions.

Hebrew nouns have a gender, and gender helps predict the plural. As a rule, masculine nouns add -im and feminine nouns add -ot. A son becomes sons, and a land becomes lands. This is only a tendency. Some masculine nouns take -ot, and some feminine nouns take -im, and the stem often shifts its vowels when the ending is added, because the stress moves. The plural is therefore best learned together with the singular. The examples are chosen from the vocabulary list, which records a gender and a plural for each noun, and the rule is simply counted over that list. Because the list was built by a program, some entries may be wrong, so treat the count as a guide. Look at the ending first, then at what happened to the vowels in the stem.
Many Hebrew words are built on a skeleton of usually three consonants that carries a core meaning.

Most Hebrew words are built on a root, a skeleton of usually three consonants that carries a core idea. Vowels and extra letters are woven around the root to make verbs, nouns and adjectives that feel related. If you know the root for write, you can often guess that a related noun has something to do with writing. Roots help you remember words in families instead of one at a time. The examples group real words from the vocabulary list that share a recorded root. Do not treat a root as a guarantee: related words can drift far apart in meaning, and some roots have weak letters that disappear in certain forms. The vocabulary list was built by a program, so a recorded root may occasionally be wrong. Use the families below as a memory aid, and match each word to the root it belongs to.
How prayers begin: common opening patterns
Many prayer lines start with one of a few stock openings, such as the blessing formula.

Many Hebrew prayers start with a stock opening, so learning a handful of them lets you recognise hundreds of lines. The most common is the blessing formula, which begins with the word for blessed, then you, then the divine name, then our God and king of the world. After that comes a closing clause that says what the blessing is for, such as bringing forth bread or creating the fruit of the vine. Other lines open with a call to listen, with a word for happy or fortunate, with a plea such as lord of the world, or with a word meaning who. The examples below are the first words of real lines in the reading library. Each one shows the English of the line beside it. Match the opening to the meaning, and notice how often the first word alone gives away the type of prayer.

From Friday afternoon until Saturday night, many shops, restaurants and offices close. Buses and trains generally do not run on Shabbat in most places. Plan food and transport before Friday afternoon.
On Friday people say shabbat shalom. After Shabbat ends, shavua tov ('a good week') is the greeting. Before a festival, chag sameach is common.

Many restaurants display a kashrut certificate. 'Basari' means meat, 'chalavi' means dairy, and 'parve' means neither. Meat and dairy are not mixed in a kosher place. Some places are not kosher: check the sign.
At a restaurant with table service, a tip of roughly ten to fifteen percent is commonly given when service is not already added to the bill. Check the bill. Tipping at a counter is less usual.
General impression of practice; check the current norm with a local.
Rounding up a taxi fare is welcome but is not an obligation. Ask for the meter or agree the price first when there is no meter.
Not verified; check with a local.

At a market stall, asking for a better price is often accepted, especially for non-food goods. Prices of fruit and vegetables sold by the kilo are usually posted. In a shop with price tags, do not haggle.
Many learners report that Israelis are direct: short questions, quick answers and strong opinions are common. This is not always rudeness. Reply in the same plain way and add bevakasha and toda.
A common description, not a measured fact.
Some malls, stations and public venues check bags at the entrance. Have your bag open and be patient.
Common in practice, but not every venue.
At synagogues, churches, mosques and the Western Wall, cover shoulders and knees, and follow signs and staff. Men may be asked to cover their heads at some Jewish sites.
The Rav-Kav is a rechargeable transit card used across public transport. Ask staff or check the official site for where to buy and top it up.
Details about where to buy and load were not verified.
What is spoken in Tel Aviv?

Everyday life in Tel Aviv is conducted in modern Hebrew, the same language as elsewhere in Israel, with casual forms and slang like the words on the fillers page. Visitors often report that English is widely understood, and some people may reply to you in English. How a local sounds depends on age, background and neighbourhood.
General impressions, not measured; regional variation not verified.

Every Hebrew noun is masculine or feminine. A noun ending in -a is usually feminine, and the adjective must match it.
When you learn a noun, learn it with its adjective ending: misada tova.

Memory hooks written for Aleph (revision 2: weak hooks rewritten, altStory + soundAnchor + caption added). Letter-name meanings (bayit = house, yad = hand, kof = monkey, ayin = eye) are ordinary Hebrew words and are reliable. The idea that each letter once DREW that object in ancient scripts is a popular teaching story that is only partly supported, so every such remark is phrased as 'often taught as' and never as proven history. Several name meanings (tet, chet, tsadi, nun) are uncertain and are marked so. The stories are memory hooks, not etymology: they rely on English sound-alike words, and the shape descriptions refer to the modern square print letter. Sounds are modern Israeli values, except ayin, which names the Israeli, Ashkenazi and Sephardi readings separately because data/pronunciation/consonants.json lists them differently. Example words are pointed by hand and need native proofreading. No Hebrew appears inside image ideas: Hebrew is overlaid as vector text.

Each letter gets (1) a shape hook, (2) a sound anchor (an English word that starts with the sound), (3) a quirky story that ties shape and sound to one picture, (4) a second story to use if the first does not stick (altStory), (5) a look-alike warning, (6) a pointed anchor word, (7) a one-line caption for the printable workbook. Based on the keyword-mnemonic idea (embedded picture + sound), Shmidman & Ehri 2010; effect size not verified here.

What Reform Jews hold on to, what they leave to personal choice, and how the movement has written down its beliefs over time.
teaching; the Five Books of Moses

Reform Judaism keeps three old ideas at its centre: God, Torah and Israel. Israel here means the Jewish people, not only the country. Around that centre, Reform Jews believe and practise in many different ways, and the movement says so openly.
In North America the movement is led by the Union for Reform Judaism. Its rabbis belong to the Central Conference of American Rabbis, and that body has written the movement's statements of belief.

Reform rabbis have put their beliefs on paper several times. The first was the Pittsburgh Platform of 1885. Later statements came in 1937 in Columbus, in 1976 in San Francisco and in 1999, again in Pittsburgh.

Each one reads differently, and that is the point. The 1885 text set aside much of traditional ritual. The 1999 statement invited Reform Jews to look again at traditional practice and choose what gives their lives holiness. You can read every one of these documents on the rabbis' own website.

A Reform Jew is asked to learn first, then make thoughtful choices about how to live out Jewish values, weighing each mitzvah on its merits. The movement says plainly that there is more than one real way to be Jewish.

The movement also puts a lot of weight on repairing the world, which it calls tikkun olam. And it works to welcome everyone: in 2015 it affirmed full inclusion of people of all gender identities and gender expressions.

Candles, wine, two loaves and a blessing for the children: the Friday night table, step by step, and why each piece is there.

Shabbat starts at sundown on Friday. It ends on Saturday evening with Havdalah, a few minutes of blessings over wine, spices and a braided candle that mark the line between the holy day and the week.
People greet each other with Shabbat shalom, a wish for a peaceful Sabbath.

Most homes light at least two candles. The Torah tells us about Shabbat twice, once to remember it (Exodus 20:8) and once to keep it (Deuteronomy 5:12), and each candle stands for one of those verses.
Here's a detail that surprises people: the candles are lit first and the blessing comes after. Saying the blessing is what begins Shabbat, so you light while it is still a weekday.
Kiddush comes next, said over wine. Grape juice works just as well for children or anyone who doesn't drink.

Then two whole loaves of challah. They recall the double portion of manna that fell in the desert before each Sabbath, so no one had to gather food on the day of rest (Exodus 16). Many families also bless their children at the table, using words from Genesis 48:20.
After that, eat slowly. The meal itself is part of the day.

Months that follow the moon, years that follow the sun, and the extra month that keeps Passover in spring.

A Hebrew month, a chodesh, runs from one new moon to the next, so it lasts 29 or 30 days. Its first day is called Rosh Chodesh, the head of the month. Twelve of those months add up to about 354 days.

The sun's year is longer, roughly 365 and a quarter days. Left alone, a calendar of moon months would slip about 11 days earlier every year, and the spring festival of Passover would wander into winter, then autumn.

The fix is to add a whole month now and then. Seven times in every 19 years, the year gets a second month of Adar. The two are called Adar I and Adar II, and Hebrew calls that kind of year shanah me'uberet, a pregnant year.
Tradition credits a sage named Hillel II with fixing this 19-year cycle in advance, and the same system is still used. In those years Purim, normally on the 14th of Adar, is kept in Adar II.
A Jewish day begins at sunset, not midnight. That's why Shabbat and every festival start in the evening, and why the calendar in Aleph marks the evening before each holy day.

Ten days that start with a new year and end with a fast: what teshuvah means and what you'll hear and see in the synagogue.

Rosh HaShanah, the Jewish new year, falls on the first of Tishrei. It opens ten days called the Days of Awe, and those days close with Yom Kippur on the tenth.

The theme of the whole stretch is teshuvah. The word means turning, and the idea is practical: notice where you went wrong, make it right with the people involved, and come back to the person you want to be.

A shofar is a ram's horn, and its raw sound is the signature of the season. It is blown during the month of Elul as a reminder that the holy days are coming, on Rosh HaShanah itself, and one last time when Yom Kippur ends.
On the first day, often in the afternoon, many people go to a river or other moving water for Tashlich. They toss in bits of bread as a picture of casting away the year's wrongs.
Yom Kippur is the most solemn day of the year. Many adults fast from evening to evening and spend much of the day in prayer. More people come to synagogue on these days than at any other time.
Most Reform congregations keep one day of Rosh HaShanah, though a growing number now keep two.

Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah
A week in a hut with a leafy roof, a bundle of branches and a citron, and a party for the Torah at the end.

Five days after Yom Kippur comes Sukkot, a harvest festival. It also recalls the forty years the Israelites spent in the desert after leaving Egypt, living in shelters that could be taken down and moved.
So people build a sukkah, a hut with a roof of branches, and eat their meals in it for the week. The Torah's own instruction is short: live in booths for seven days (Leviticus 23:42).

Sukkot's other symbol is held in two hands. The lulav is a palm branch bound with myrtle and willow; the etrog is a citron. After a blessing they are waved in six directions: east, south, west, north, up and down.

On the eighth day comes Shemini Atzeret. Reform congregations and Jews in Israel celebrate Simchat Torah on that same day. The last lines of Deuteronomy are read, then the first lines of Genesis straight after, so the reading never really stops. People sing and dance with the Torah scrolls.

A rededicated Temple, a later story about oil, and eight nights of lights in the window.

Hanukkah means dedication. In the second century before the common era, a Jewish rebel group led by the Maccabees won Jerusalem back from its Syrian-Greek rulers and rededicated the Temple. They celebrated for eight days, matching the eight days of Sukkot.
Hanukkah isn't in the Torah. The sages added it later, and it begins on the 25th of Kislev.

The famous story of a small jar of oil that burned for eight days doesn't appear in the books of the Maccabees. It shows up centuries later, in the Talmud. Both stories are part of the holiday now, and many families tell them side by side.

The hanukkiyah has nine branches: eight for the nights and one, the shamash, that lights the rest. You light one candle the first night and add one each night until all eight are burning. The lamp goes in a window or by the door so people passing can see it.
Foods fried in oil, like latkes and doughnuts, belong to the same story.

Purim and the Book of Esther
A noisy reading of a scroll, food for friends and money for people in need: the four things Purim asks of you.

The Book of Esther tells of a Persian court where an official named Haman plots to destroy the Jews. Queen Esther and her cousin Mordecai turn the plot around. Purim falls on the 14th of Adar, and in a leap year it moves to Adar II.
The book is read aloud from a scroll called the megillah, and the room makes as much noise as it can every time Haman's name comes up.
Four duties belong to the day, as the rabbis listed them: hear the megillah, send food to friends, give to people in need, and sit down to a festive meal.
Mishloach manot, the food gift, has a simple rule: at least two kinds of ready-to-eat food, to at least one person. Three-cornered cookies called hamantaschen are a favourite.

Pesach remembers the Exodus, the Israelites' escape from slavery in Egypt. Its heart is the seder, a festive home meal. Seder means order, because the evening follows a fixed sequence of about fifteen steps, from blessing the wine to songs at the end.
The steps are written out in a book called the Haggadah, which means the telling. Many versions exist, from traditional to playful, and many congregations also hold a community seder.

A special plate sits near whoever leads. On it you'll usually find a roasted shank bone, an egg, a green vegetable such as parsley, a bitter herb, lettuce, and charoset, a sweet mix of fruit and nuts. Each one is pointed to and explained during the evening.

Shavuot means weeks. It comes seven weeks after Pesach, which links leaving Egypt with arriving at Mount Sinai.

It began as a harvest festival, when the first fruits were brought to the Temple. The link to matan Torah, the giving of the Torah, came later, after the Temple was destroyed. The Torah itself doesn't make that connection.
Many synagogues read the Book of Ruth. Ruth chose to join the Jewish people, and one reason given for reading her story now is that, like the Israelites at Sinai, she took on the covenant herself.
Dairy food is traditional, cheesecake and blintzes especially. People connect it with the sweetness of Torah and with the land the Torah calls flowing with milk and honey (Exodus 3:8).
Reform congregations often hold confirmation on or near Shavuot, for teenagers who kept studying after their bar or bat mitzvah.

Open a siddur, a prayer book, at the morning service and you'll find it begins with short blessings of thanks for ordinary things and a set of psalms. These were first said at home while getting up and dressing. They help you arrive before the main prayers start.

Then the leader calls the room to prayer with Barchu, and the congregation answers. Two blessings follow, one about creation and one about the gift of Torah. Then comes the Shema itself: Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One (Deuteronomy 6:4). One more blessing after it gives thanks for freedom from Egypt.
The Shema is said morning and evening. It isn't a request at all. It's a statement that God is one.

Next is the Amidah, which means standing, because you say it on your feet. It opens with praise and closes with thanks. On weekdays the middle holds requests; on Shabbat those are left out and the middle is about the day itself.
Many people say it quietly, at their own pace. Saying it in English is fine, and so is adding words of your own.
On Shabbat morning, and briefly on Mondays and Thursdays, a Torah scroll is taken out and read. The service then winds down with Aleinu, the Mourner's Kaddish and a closing song such as Adon Olam.

The Torah, the Five Books of Moses, is split into 54 portions. Each one is a parashah. Each one takes its name from its first distinctive word or words. The first portion is Bereishit, which means in the beginning.
One portion is chanted from the scroll each Shabbat morning. A regular year has fewer Shabbatot than portions, so a few short ones are read in pairs to finish on time.
The cycle ends and starts again on Simchat Torah. The last verses of Deuteronomy are read and the first of Genesis follow right away, so the scroll never sits finished.
After the Torah comes the haftarah, a reading from the Prophets picked to echo the week's portion.
The reading is divided into sections, and members of the congregation are invited up to say a blessing before and after each one. That honour is called an aliyah, which means going up.

For centuries Hebrew was for prayer and study. Then one stubborn family started speaking it at breakfast.

Hebrew, Ivrit, never disappeared. Jews prayed in it, studied in it and wrote letters about religious questions in it. What it had lost, for many centuries, was everyday speech: nobody grew up talking about breakfast or the weather in Hebrew.

Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, born in 1858 in the village of Luzhky, set out to change that. He reached Jerusalem in 1881 and, with his wife Deborah, made their home a Hebrew-only home. Their son Ben-Zion became the first child in modern times raised with Hebrew as his mother tongue.
The thinking was simple. If a child could grow up speaking Hebrew, a whole people could.

Ben-Yehuda pushed for Hebrew as the language of teaching in schools, which turned out to matter most. He ran newspapers, invented words for modern things and began a huge dictionary in 1910 that took seventeen volumes and was finished long after his death in 1922.
He also helped found the Hebrew Language Committee, Va'ad HaLashon, which grew into today's Academy of the Hebrew Language. When you learn a word like milon in Aleph, you're using his work.

Vancouver's only Reform congregation, founded in 1965; its first home was firebombed in 1985 and the Oak Street synagogue opened in 1988.

Temple Sholom was founded in 1965 and is Vancouver's only Reform congregation. For its first decade it held services in members' living rooms and basements. In 1976 it bought a former Masonic hall at 4426 West 10th Avenue, between Trimble and Sasamat, and made that its first permanent home. Rabbi Philip Bregman joined the congregation in 1980 and would go on to serve it for most of his career; he is now rabbi emeritus.

In January 1985 an arsonist threw a Molotov cocktail through a window of the West 10th Avenue building. The fire destroyed much of the ground floor; most of the prayer books and all but one of the Torah scrolls were saved. A menorah of wood and metal that stood beside the window came through the blaze unburnt, something neither the rabbi nor the fire crew could explain, and it now stands in the Oak Street synagogue as a reminder of hope in dark times. The attackers were never found.

With support from Mayor Mike Harcourt and from across the Jewish community, two lots were bought on Oak Street between 54th and 57th Avenues, in the corridor where most of Vancouver's Jewish institutions had gathered since the 1940s. The new synagogue, designed by Richard Henriquez, was completed and occupied in June 1988.

Rabbi Dan Moskovitz has been senior rabbi since 2013. Membership stood at more than 600 households that year and grew by more than half over the following nine years. For its 50th anniversary in 2015 the members fulfilled the 613th commandment together by scribing a new Anniversary Torah. Temple Sholom belongs to the Western Canadian Reform Collaboration with the Reform congregations of Calgary, Edmonton, Victoria and Winnipeg.

Kolot Mayim, Hebrew for 'Voices of the Water', is the Reform congregation of Victoria and Vancouver Island. It was founded in 1998 by a small group of individuals and families who met monthly in living rooms and at the Victoria Jewish Community Centre. The JCC on Shelbourne Street in Saanich is still its home.

Lynn Greenhough, a long-standing figure in Victoria's Jewish life, became the congregation's spiritual leader in 2017 while completing rabbinical studies through the Jewish Spiritual Leaders Institute. She was installed as rabbi on 6 September 2019, the first Canadian-born rabbi to serve the Greater Victoria community.

The congregation is known for its free public lecture series. Building Bridges, a six-part series held mostly on Sunday mornings over Zoom, began in the 2021-22 season with the theme Celebrating Diversity in Jewish Life and has returned every year since, alongside the Kvell at the Well and L'dor V'dor series. Speakers have included rabbis, historians, genealogists and musicians from across North America.

Kolot Mayim is an inclusive and welcoming community, focused on learning and on celebrating Jewish life. It belongs to the Western Canadian Reform Collaboration with the Reform congregations of Vancouver, Calgary, Edmonton and Winnipeg.

Calgary's Reform congregation began on 6 April 1979 with a Shabbat service in the living room of Ron and Judy Bing: 33 people from 13 families. Norm Yanofsky played guitar and Henry Zimmer read the weekly Torah portion. The group incorporated that year as the Calgary Liberal Jewish Congregation and in 1980 took the name Temple B'nai Tikvah, 'Children of Hope', suggested by member Steven Switzer.

In March 1980 Ron Bing collected a donated Torah scroll, shipped in a wooden crate, from the customs office at Calgary's airport; it was dedicated that May at a service in the basement of the Fagan family home. For its first quarter-century the congregation had no building of its own and moved through members' homes, a library and the Calgary Jewish Centre.

On 21 February 2004 members carried their Torah scrolls in procession to a new home in the Britannia neighbourhood: the former Riverview United Church, a Modern-style building of 1957, which they shared at first with Living Spirit United Church. The first service there was held on 27 February 2004. The Temple took full ownership of the building in 2007, and the sanctuary in the converted church was dedicated on 25 March 2011.

The congregation's first full-time rabbi, Jordan Goldson, arrived in 1987 and was Alberta's first full-time Reform rabbi. Today the Temple runs Shabbatots for three- and four-year-olds, a Saturday-morning Shabbat School from preschool to Grade 7, and a two-year b'nai mitzvah program. Community service has long been part of its life: for many years it regularly hosted a shelter through Calgary's Inn from the Cold, and it set up a refugee assistance committee in 2016. It belongs to the Western Canadian Reform Collaboration.

Edmonton's only Reform synagogue, founded in 1979 by three families and housed since 2007 at Chesed Shel Emeth in Westmount.

Temple Beth Ora was founded in 1979 as Beth Ora Synagogue, when three Edmonton families decided they wanted a Reform Jewish presence in the city. It was incorporated in 1980, the year its Beit Sefer classes began, and it became the Edmonton community's third congregation after the Orthodox Beth Israel and the Conservative Beth Shalom. It remains the city's only Reform synagogue.

The congregation has never built a home of its own. For many years it rented space and held services in the Jewish Community Centre building overlooking the North Saskatchewan River. In 2007 it moved to Chesed Shel Emeth, the chapel of Edmonton's Chevra Kadisha at 123 Street and 105 Avenue in the Westmount neighbourhood, where it is still based.

Temple Beth Ora is affiliated with the Union for Reform Judaism. Rabbi Gila Caine was installed in April 2018 at a service that filled the sanctuary. The congregation takes part in the Western Canadian Reform Collaboration, a joint effort of the Reform synagogues of Edmonton, Calgary, Vancouver, Victoria and Winnipeg.

Winnipeg's only Reform synagogue, opened in 1965 and settled at Grant Avenue and Wilton since 1987.

Temple Shalom is Winnipeg's only Reform synagogue. It opened in the city's south end in 1965, its beginnings owing much to an influx of university professors who had grown up in Reform congregations elsewhere and wanted one of their own. In a city where Reform is one of the smallest streams rather than the largest, the Temple stands out, and for many of its members it is their one formal connection to Jewish life.

After years of effort the congregation established a permanent home at the corner of Grant Avenue and Wilton Street in 1987. Rabbi Eric Silver said at the time that it was 'a place we can call our own'. The Temple has a record as an innovator: in September 1984 its Rabbi Tracy Klirs became the first woman to lead a Canadian congregation as its rabbi, and it was the first congregation in Winnipeg to perform same-sex and interfaith marriages.

Alongside Shabbat and holy-day services with a strong musical tradition, the Temple runs the Irma Penn School for Judaic Studies, an Introduction to Judaism course and adult education. Its affiliated cemetery, Beit Chayim Mikdash Shalom, serves Jews by birth, Jews by choice and interfaith families according to Reform practice.

The Reaching Out Reaching Up capital campaign, launched on 5 November 2017, raised $400,000 in its first month; the same year the congregation set up an endowment fund with the Jewish Foundation of Manitoba. Rabbi Allan Finkel initiated the Western Canadian Reform Collaboration linking Winnipeg with the Reform congregations of Calgary, Edmonton, Vancouver and Victoria. Rabbi Myriam Saitman's installation was scheduled for 21 November 2025.

Canada's oldest Reform congregation (1882) and the only one left in Quebec; its present Sherbrooke Street sanctuary was dedicated in 1960.

Temple Emanu-El is the oldest Liberal or Reform congregation in Canada and today the only Reform congregation in Quebec. Its founding meeting was held on 23 August 1882 at Lindsay Hall on St. Catherine Street West, and it was incorporated by an act of the Quebec legislature on 30 March 1883. Rabbi Samuel Marks served as its first minister from 1882 to 1889, and early services were held at Albert Hall in Zion Church on Beaver Hall Hill. In 1892 the congregation built its first temple, seating about 275, at Stanley and Cypress Streets downtown.

By 1910 the downtown site was too small. A Byzantine Revival temple designed by John Melville Miller, seating 700, was dedicated at Elm Avenue and Sherbrooke Street in Westmount in September 1911; it was enlarged in 1922, and a community house by C. Davis Goodman with an auditorium, offices and a larger school was added in 1940-41. In 1953 the Aron Museum opened in the building as Canada's first museum of Jewish ceremonial art, and the same year about fifty families left to found Temple Beth Sholom in Notre-Dame-de-Grace, Montreal's second Reform congregation.

In December 1957 the 1911 temple burned down. A new Modernist building by architect Max Roth rose on the site and was dedicated on 22 April 1960, led by Rabbi Harry Joshua Stern, who served the congregation from 1927 to 1979. Temple Beth Sholom rejoined its parent in 1980 to form Temple Emanu-El-Beth Sholom, and in 1992 Temple Rodeph Shalom merged in as well; the chapel was renamed in its honour.

Rabbi Bernard Bloomstone led the merged congregation from 1972 to 1983 and Rabbi Leigh Lerner from March 1989 until 2012, when he became rabbi emeritus and Rabbi Lisa Grushcow succeeded him. Rachelle Shubert has been director of music and cantorial soloist since 2001. The Temple offers cemetery services at four locations including Mount Royal Cemetery, runs the Westmount Mini Centre with the Cummings Jewish Centre for Seniors, and is affiliated with the Union for Reform Judaism and the Canadian Association of Reform Zionists.

B'nai Shalom v'Tikvah, 'Children of Peace and Hope', grew out of Jewish Families of Durham, a social group whose members had come to the region from Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver and from Reform, Conservative and Orthodox backgrounds. The idea of a synagogue of their own came up at one of the group's meetings; after polling the members, a Reform congregation was chosen and formally established in May 1994 as the Durham Region Reform Synagogue, the first Reform synagogue in Durham.

Like the wandering Israelites, as the congregation puts it, it moved around for a few years before settling at St. Paul's United Church on Kings Crescent in Ajax, where it still worships. It has grown to about 50 membership units, a tight-knit but welcoming group serving Ajax, Pickering, Whitby and the wider Durham Region.
The congregation holds Shabbat and festival services, runs a Hebrew school, marks life-cycle events and offers funeral and burial services. Its website names Rabbi Printz as its rabbi.

The only synagogue in Barrie and Simcoe County, grown from the Simcoe County Jewish Association and housed since 2003 in a building on donated land.

For about forty years the Jewish families of Simcoe County met as the Simcoe County Jewish Association, gathering for holiday services and events in one another's homes and in rented premises. Members lived not only in Barrie but in Collingwood, Gravenhurst and other towns across the region. By 2000 the community had grown to about 100 families, had raised $100,000 of its own money toward a first synagogue, and drew 150 people to Yom Kippur services; that July it received a Torah scroll donated by B'nai Tikvah Congregation in Niagara Falls.

The association was renamed Am Shalom Congregation in 2001. Henry Bernick, a developer who had grown up in the Barrie area, donated land on Huronia Road at Lockhart Road in the city's south end, and with further donations a 10,000-square-foot synagogue was completed there in 2003. Some accounts give 2004 as the year the congregation in its present form began.

Am Shalom is a Reform congregation affiliated with the Union for Reform Judaism, with about 75 member families. As the only synagogue in Barrie and Simcoe County it also serves Muskoka, Collingwood, Innisfil, Newmarket and the surrounding area. It runs the Jewish Heritage School for children from age four to bar and bat mitzvah, Shabbat and holiday services, adult education and a choir, Shirat Am Shalom, and takes part in interfaith and educational outreach in the wider community. The Reform rabbis' council lists Rabbi Emma Gottlieb as its rabbi from May 2025.

Brampton's only synagogue, begun with a tea for Jewish women in 1977; for decades it worshipped in an 1876 church it bought in 1983.

Har Tikvah, 'Mountain of Hope', began in September 1977 with a tea for the Jewish women of North Peel. The group incorporated in 1978 as the North Peel Jewish Association, and the congregation dates its service to the Jewish community of North Peel and Halton from 1979. It took the name Har Tikvah and joined the Reform movement in 1981.

In 1983 the congregation bought the former Harrison United Church at 9893 Torbram Road, built in 1876 as a Methodist church on land donated by John Stubbings, and converted it into a synagogue. On 13 August 1984 the City of Brampton designated the building under the Ontario Heritage Act for its historical and architectural value. Land to the north was bought in 1998 to allow for growth, and in 1999 portables were moved onto the site to house the Hebrew school.

Har Tikvah now worships at 380 Bovaird Drive East. It is the only synagogue in Brampton and serves Brampton, Bramalea, Bolton, Malton, Georgetown and Caledon with Shabbat and festival services, a Hebrew school for ages three to sixteen, Torah study, adult education, speakers and bar and bat mitzvah tutoring. It is a member of the Union for Reform Judaism and the Reform Jewish Community of Canada, and its rabbi is Michal Shekel.

Canada's first Reform congregation and Ontario's oldest Jewish congregation, formed by Hamilton's German Jewish families in 1853.

Hamilton's first Jewish families began gathering for communal life over a store on James Street South in 1850, when the city counted some thirteen to sixteen Jewish households, mostly German. In 1853 they formed the Hebrew Benevolent Society Anshe-Sholom of Hamilton. Services began in 1856, a half-acre cemetery plot was bought the following year, and on 5 May 1863 the Jewish Congregation Anshe-Sholom of Hamilton was incorporated with nineteen founding members; the early records were kept in German. In 1866 a room above a leather goods shop downtown became its first formal synagogue.

Edmund Scheuer arrived from Paris in 1871 to join his brother-in-law's jewellery business, served as president from 1873 to 1886, founded and taught the religious school, and led Anshe Sholom into the Reform movement in 1882, earning the name 'father of Canadian Reform Judaism'. In 1874 the women of the congregation, led by his sister Camilla Levy, formed the Deborah Ladies Aid Society, the first Jewish women's charitable society in Canada. The Hughson Street Temple, dedicated in 1882, served the congregation for almost seventy years.

After the Second World War Anshe Sholom became the first Hamilton synagogue to follow its members westward. The present building on Cline Avenue North in Westdale, designed by Joseph Singer, was built in 1951 and dedicated in June 1952; a new wing with a school section was added in 1963. Rabbi Bernard Baskin held the pulpit for a record forty years, and Rabbi Jordan D. Cohen, the congregation's first Canadian-born rabbi, began his service on 1 January 2007. Louise Sole Rotman was the first woman to serve as president.

Recognised as Canada's first Reform congregation and Ontario's oldest Jewish congregation, Temple Anshe Sholom marked its 170th anniversary in 2020. Its worship is traditional yet innovative, and it is committed to the full equality of women and the full participation of LGBTQ members. Nearly four metres of its records are held by the Ontario Jewish Archives.

Kingston's Reform congregation, 'City of the King', organised around Rosh Hashanah 1975 by Queen's University families.

A new chapter in Kingston's Jewish life opened in 1975 when a Reform congregation was organised, thanks in large part to Michael Levison, a recently arrived British Jew and pioneering computer scientist at Queen's University. The first organising meeting was held around Rosh Hashanah that year, and the first services on 26 September 1975 in Dupuis Hall at Queen's. Just under half of the founders taught at the university. After weighing Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist options the group settled on Reform in the spring of 1976 and affiliated formally the following year. It called itself Iyr Ha-Melech, Hebrew for 'City of the King', a play on the name Kingston.

The congregation grew from about ten families to around forty households and families. Between 1983 and 1993 household memberships rose from 19 to 50. In 1985 it completed the purchase of a block of plots in Cataraqui Cemetery, and in 1986 president Moussa Cohanim could write in his final report, 'We are here to stay.' Ann Levison ran the Hebrew school, members produced a lively newsletter called The Iyr Ha-Melech Whig, and part-time rabbis such as Barbara Bortz of Montreal shared the leading of services with lay members.

Iyr Ha-Melech has long held its services in halls rather than a building of its own: for years in a hall at Queen's, and now at KUF Hall on McMahon Avenue. It holds Shabbat and holiday services, prepares young people for bar and bat mitzvah, and offers an open, liberal and inclusive Judaism to Kingston and the surrounding region. Members of the Orthodox Beth Israel and of Iyr Ha-Melech sit together on the Kingston Jewish Council, and some families belong to both.

London's Reform congregation, founded in 1985 from the London Jewish Family Association and led since 2010 by the city's first full-time female rabbi.

Temple Israel was officially founded in 1985, but its roots go back a decade earlier to the London Jewish Family Association, a group of about eighteen families. Its first president was Rael Wienburg. In 1987 the congregation hired its first rabbi, Joel Wittstein, a native of Cincinnati who had first trained as a teacher; he and his wife Ailene made Temple Israel a strong voice for Reform Judaism in London and Southwestern Ontario, and under his leadership the congregation grew from 40 families to 140.

Rabbi Wittstein led the congregation until his death in January 2010 at the age of 74. Rabbi Michal Shekel of Toronto served as interim rabbi, and in June 2010 Rabbi Debra Stahlberg Dressler, newly ordained at Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati after a first career in direct marketing and magazine circulation, became the congregation's second spiritual leader and London's first full-time female rabbi. She co-founded the London Interfaith Peace Camp, which brings Jewish, Christian and Muslim young people together, and serves as principal of the religious school.

Over the years Temple Israel has called many places home: a suburban basement, a building on Adelaide Street, and now a house on Windermere Road, a former family estate. Among its Torah scrolls is one from the Memorial Scrolls Trust, scroll number 357, which the congregation reads with reverence for its history. Temple Israel is a member of the Union for Reform Judaism and the London Jewish Federation, is part of the Camp George community, and takes part in the London Multi-Faith Social Action Coalition, interfaith tree plantings and food sorts.

Mississauga's first synagogue and only Reform congregation, 'Pathfinder', founded in 1973 and settled on Folkway Drive since the last day of 1978.

In 1973, the Hebrew year 5734, there was no synagogue, rabbi or Hebrew school in Mississauga. A handful of Jewish families, strangers to one another, decided there should be a Jewish presence in the city and a Jewish experience for their children. They engaged a young student rabbi, Lawrence Englander, who came in once a month, stayed with congregants for the weekend and led services in various rented places, most memorably a dilapidated former monastery that is now the Glen Erin Inn. Lester Krames was the founding president from 1974 to 1976.

The congregation took the name Solel, 'Pathfinder', from Isaiah 62:10, 'Solu, solu! Blaze the pathway', and became the pathfinder for Jewish life in Mississauga. A larger group raised the money to buy the property at 2399 Folkway Drive in the Sawmill Valley area of Erin Mills and to build a synagogue there. On 31 December 1978 members marched, danced and sang their way from the Glen Erin Inn to the new building, which opened in 1979.

Rabbi Englander served Solel from its founding until his retirement in June 2014 and remains rabbi emeritus. He was named Mississauga's citizen of the year in 1980, appointed a Member of the Order of Canada in 2005, and helped found two interfaith institutions in the city: Foodpath, the community food bank, and Pathway Non-Profit Community Development, of which he was founding president. Rabbi Audrey Pollack succeeded him as senior rabbi in 2014.

Solel has grown to more than 300 member families and runs a religious and language school two days a week for preschoolers to adults. Since 1980 it has been twinned with Kehilat Darchei Noam in Ramat HaSharon, Israel, and it has led several missions there. The congregation celebrated its fiftieth anniversary in 2023-24, re-enacting the walk from the Glen Erin Inn to Folkway Drive.
