A small, family-like Reform congregation serving Newmarket and northern York Region since the early 1990s.

Or Hadash, 'New Light', is the Reform congregation of Newmarket and northern York Region. It has served the community since the early 1990s. Its members come from Newmarket, Aurora, Innisfil and Keswick, with some from Richmond Hill and Thornhill, and the congregation also serves Jewish families in Simcoe County and Durham Region.

For years the congregation made do with borrowed space, one year holding its High Holy Day services at a golf course. It later moved into a larger building in the heart of downtown Newmarket, near the public library, using two of the three floors for services, programming and its Hebrew school. Rabbi Jonathan Crane, who worked part-time with the congregation and led its High Holy Day services at the time, said the move gave Or Hadash a real footprint in Newmarket and in Ontario.

Or Hadash is warm, friendly and egalitarian, with a family-like atmosphere. It holds weekly Shabbat and holiday services and runs a religious school, adult education and Tikkun Olam projects. Members say that community, more than location, is what draws them. A travel directory lists Rabbi Michal Shekel as its rabbi.

Halton's only synagogue, begun by fifteen Oakville families in 1955 and built on land offered by a local farming family.

The story begins with two immigrant couples. Morris Burke left Romania in 1912, married Rose in Toronto and settled in Oakville in 1922; Michael Brown, born Marcos Zuckerman, left Bukovina the same year, married Becky and settled in Oakville in 1923. The two women, both pregnant, met at a baby clinic in town, and the idea of a Jewish congregation was conceived. In 1955 fifteen families founded the Oakville-Trafalgar Jewish Community Centre, with plans to celebrate the holidays together, give the children religious instruction, and hold poker nights for the fathers.

When the growing congregation looked for land, the Jensen family of Oakville offered the far end of what was then Morrison Farms. Donations came in, the building was finished in 1962, and the congregation renamed itself Beth El, 'House of God'. By the late 1960s it had a hundred families and hired a rabbi, and it raised money with bazaars, bingo and fashion shows in the Pine Room of the Oakville Arena.

Rabbi Edward Goldfarb, formerly director of education at Temple Sinai in Toronto, arrived in 1982 as the first full-time rabbi and found a congregation of thirty to thirty-five families struggling to survive; he served eighteen years and saw it become a permanent part of the town. In the 1980s the synagogue merged with the Burlington Jewish Group to form Shaarei-Beth El Congregation of Halton, and in 1985 a 6,000-square-foot expansion with a 250-seat sanctuary was added to the front of the original building and dedicated in 1986. Stained-glass windows on the theme of the Days of Awe honour Rabbi Goldfarb's retirement.

Rabbi Stephen Wise, a Toronto native ordained in 2005 and previously assistant rabbi at Temple Beth El in Boca Raton, took up the pulpit on 1 July 2007 and was installed that November. Shaarei Beth El is a Reform congregation with a traditional orientation, serving Oakville, Burlington and Halton Region with weekly Shabbat morning services, Friday evening services, festivals and adult education; its school is directed by Cheryl Wise. About 165 families belong. The sixtieth anniversary in November 2015 brought a welcoming address from Rabbi Rick Jacobs, president of the Union for Reform Judaism, and the first Liz Fein Memorial leadership award.

Ottawa's first and only Reform congregation, founded in the spring of 1966, in its Prince of Wales Drive synagogue since 1975.

Temple Israel, the first Reform congregation in Ottawa, was founded in the spring of 1966 by Bill and Billy Danson, Myrna and Ernie Potechin, Irwin and Elaine Singer, Sam and Jean Bond and Madelyn Alexandor. By November of that year seventeen families belonged. Early services were held in a public school. The name Temple Israel was chosen in March 1967, Rabbi David Powell arrived that summer, membership passed fifty within a year, and the first consecration service was held on 28 October 1967.

The congregation's first home of its own was the former B'nai Jacob synagogue at 54 James Street, acquired in 1971. A fire in 1972 badly damaged the building and destroyed a Czech memorial Torah scroll, number 355; a saved fragment of that scroll hangs framed in the present synagogue. Rabbi Powell served until 1972 and was followed by Rabbi Donald Gerber until 1980.

Ground was broken at 1301 Prince of Wales Drive on 27 April 1975, and that autumn the congregation held its High Holy Day services in the newly designed building. Temple Israel is now the second-largest congregation in Ottawa, with about 340 families, and the standard-bearer of Liberal Judaism in the capital. It is an active member of the Union for Reform Judaism, a founding member of Camp George, the Reform movement's summer camp in Ontario, and a supporter of ARZA Canada.

The Temple Israel Religious School was opened to non-members by a unanimous board vote on 21 April 2011. The congregation runs an Insight into Judaism course and a Liberal Judaism library, and its social action has included a baby-quilt project for Israel. Rabbi Daniel Mikelberg has led the congregation since 2019.

Kitchener-Waterloo's Reform congregation, formed in 1965, which in 1996 built The Cedars jointly with a United Church, known as Canada's first purpose-built Jewish-Christian house of worship.

Temple Shalom was formed in 1965 as the Kitchener-Waterloo Jewish Fellowship, with founders including Mavis Wyse and, soon after, Cyril Taylor. At the end of that year the group chose the name Temple Shalom and adopted a constitution, and in 1966 it affiliated with the Union of American Hebrew Congregations. For its first decades the congregation led a transient life in borrowed rooms, latterly a church basement, and was at times served by part-time ordained rabbis from Toronto.

In 1973 Temple Shalom elected Ethel Fahidy as president, the first woman to lead a Reform congregation in Canada. Because non-Jewish spouses and the children of interfaith marriages could not be buried in the Orthodox cemetery of Beth Jacob, the congregation acquired a section of the City of Waterloo's Parkview Cemetery in 1978, open to any Reform Jew and to their non-Jewish spouses and children.

The most significant step in its history came in 1996, when it moved into The Cedars at 543 Beechwood Drive, a $1.4 million worship and community centre designed and built jointly with Westminster United Church, a congregation formed in 1990 that had been meeting in a school gym. The partnership began when temple president Mark Pancer found himself a neighbour of a member of the church's building committee. It is known as Canada's first purpose-built Jewish-Christian house of worship, and the arrangement has worked well: the Temple worships on Friday evenings and Saturday mornings, the church on Sundays, and when Christmas Eve falls on a Friday the church simply holds a later service.

At the time of the move the congregation numbered about 68 families; by 1999 it had 75 families and a religious school of 45 students, who met weekly with the pupils of the Beth Jacob day school. Today young families from Kitchener-Waterloo, Cambridge, Guelph, Stratford and Hanover come to its Tots program and its twice-weekly religious school.

Windsor's only Reform congregation, conceived in a living room in 1959, whose first rabbi later founded Humanistic Judaism.

Congregation Beth El was conceived in the winter of 1959, when four Windsor families met in the living room of Madelyn and Arthur Weingarden with Rabbi David Baylinson, assistant rabbi of Temple Beth El in Detroit, to consider a Reform congregation for their city. Some had left the Orthodox Shaar Hashomayim over its refusal to allow mixed seating. Dr. Richard Hertz, Detroit's senior rabbi, soon met a hundred interested Windsor Jews to explain why they should found a congregation of their own, and the first services were held at Southwood School in the spring of 1960, on 15 April. The Detroit temple remained its model and close partner.

The congregation's first rabbi, serving on weekends, was Sherwin Wine, another Detroit assistant, who in 1963 would found the Birmingham Temple and with it Humanistic Judaism. A large house on Ouellette Avenue served as an early home. In 1961 the congregation accepted a gift of land and left the downtown; the cornerstone of the present synagogue on Mark Avenue was laid in July 1962, and an addition followed in 1981.

Rabbi Jonathan Plaut served from 1970 to 1984 and was instrumental in building the congregation; Rabbi Jeffrey Ableser followed. Though Reform, Beth El has always kept a strong feeling for Jewish tradition: it affiliated with the Windsor Jewish Community Council and the Va'ad HaKashruth, worked with the Orthodox congregations to obtain a cemetery, and in later years shared bar and bat mitzvah celebrations with Shaar Hashomayim. It marked its fiftieth year in October 2010 and its sixtieth in 2020.

Today Congregation Beth El runs a small Sunday-morning religious school, joins in interfaith programs with local police and faith groups, and has partnered with Temple Israel in London, Ontario, for shared seders and events; in 2022 a student rabbi from Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati visited once a month.

The Reform congregation of residents and families at Baycrest, Toronto's Jewish seniors' centre, worshipping in The Terraces.

Beth Chaverim, 'House of Friends', is the Reform congregation serving the residents, families and staff of Baycrest, Toronto's centre for geriatric care and research on Bathurst Street. It worships in the Common Room on the lower level of The Terraces, the Baycrest residence, and was earlier listed as the Baycrest Terrace Reform Congregation, 'a reform congregation of dedicated senior citizens'. The space is wheelchair accessible, with barrier-free washrooms, a Shabbat elevator, a bimah that wheelchairs can reach and large-print prayer books.

Beth Chaverim is a member congregation of the Union for Reform Judaism, and its rabbi is Rena Arshinoff. Because it meets inside a care home rather than in a building of its own, many people do not know it is there, and it warmly welcomes visiting family members.

No founding narrative or date has been found online. Baycrest itself traces its origins to the Toronto Jewish Old Folks Home of 1918; the congregation is reached through Baycrest's spiritual care office.

Downtown Toronto's Reform congregation, founded in October 2012 by Rabbi Elyse Goldstein and worshipping in borrowed church halls near the University of Toronto.

City Shul was founded in October 2012 by Rabbi Elyse Goldstein as a Reform congregation for downtown Toronto, a part of the city whose Jewish population had grown while its synagogues sat far to the north along Bathurst Street. It was formally accepted as a member of the Union for Reform Judaism in December 2013.

The congregation has never owned a building. Until September 2017 it met at the Wolfond Centre for Jewish Campus Life near the St. George campus of the University of Toronto; from 2017 to 2022 at Bloor Street United Church; and since then at St George by the Grange on Stephanie Street, beside the Art Gallery of Ontario.

City Shul is fully egalitarian and developed its own prayer book, Siddur Shirat HaLev. Rabbi Goldstein, who had earlier served as assistant rabbi at Holy Blossom Temple from 1983 to 1986, is now rabbi emerita.

Toronto's oldest Jewish congregation (1856) and the largest Reform congregation in Canada, in its landmark Bathurst Street temple since 1938.

Holy Blossom Temple dates its history to September 1856, when Lewis Samuel, an immigrant from York, England, and seventeen Jewish families from Britain and Europe met to form a congregation and plan High Holy Day services; a Toronto Hebrew Congregation had already been holding services in homes since 1849 and had founded the Pape Avenue cemetery, Toronto's first Jewish burial ground, which passed to the new congregation in 1858. The Ontario Heritage Trust recognises Holy Blossom as the first Jewish congregation in Ontario, and in 2001 placed a plaque there.

text: The congregation built its first synagogue on Richmond Street in 1876 and, having outgrown it, an elegant twin-domed temple on Bond Street in 1897, which is now a Greek Orthodox church. Founded as an Orthodox congregation, it moved toward Reform through decades of argument; Edmund Scheuer, the Hamilton reformer, led the campaign after moving to Toronto, and the congregation joined the Reform movement in the 1920s. In the 1930s it bought land on what was then the city's outer edge, and its third home at 1950 Bathurst Street, a Romanesque Revival building by Chapman and Oxley with Maurice D. Klein whose reinforced-concrete frame allows a sanctuary without columns, was dedicated on 20 May 1938.

Rabbi Abraham Feinberg, who arrived in 1943 with educator Heinz Warschauer, led the congregation through its years of greatest growth until 1961 and made it a flagship of Reform Judaism; Thurgood Marshall spoke from its pulpit in February 1955. Rabbi W. Gunther Plaut, the long-serving senior rabbi and author of the Reform movement's Torah commentary, died in 2012 at 99. In 1980 Joan Friedman became the first woman to serve as a rabbi in Canada when she was appointed assistant rabbi, and Elyse Goldstein, later founder of City Shul, served as assistant rabbi from 1983 to 1986.

With more than 7,000 members, Holy Blossom is Canada's largest Reform congregation. Rabbi Yael Splansky is senior rabbi and Rabbi John Moscowitz is rabbi emeritus. A renewal of the Bathurst Street building by Diamond Schmitt Architects, which added the Schwartz-Reisman Atrium and new accessible spaces while preserving the 1938 sanctuary, won a Platinum Reconstruction Award in 2020. The Temple's archives hold board minutes back to 1856.

A small North York Reform congregation on a wooded six-acre site, shaped by decades of social action under Rabbi Arthur Bielfeld.

Temple Emanu-El was born of the suburban growth of Toronto's Jewish community in the mid-1950s, when a handful of like-minded Reform Jews began gathering in the basement of a church. Its fiftieth-anniversary publication of 2008 implies a founding around 1958. Ground was broken at 120 Old Colony Road, in what is now North York, on 6 September 1960, and the building on its six-and-a-half-acre landscaped site was completed in 1963. In 1969-70 Temple Emanu-El and a second young Reform congregation, Beth-El, blended into one, a match the congregation calls made in heaven.

For most of its history the Temple was led by Rabbi Arthur Bielfeld, under whom it became known for social action: help for American draft resisters during the Vietnam War, early campaigning for Soviet Jewry from 1972, anti-racism work, support for former prisoners, and a role in founding Leo Baeck Day School, the Reform day school of Toronto.

Temple Emanu-El has about 360 members. Its grounds hold a Biblical Garden, and the building a quiet reading room. The Centre for Jewish Living and Learning at the Temple runs a school from pre-kindergarten to Grade 12 with a b'nai mitzvah program, and the Temple is the registered home of ARZA Canada, the Canadian Reform Zionist association.
A red-brick synagogue with a round rose window on its high front, a white-edged canopy of arched bays along the entrance and a curving drive across a lawn.
Founded in 1954 by fourteen families and a student rabbi who stayed forty years; now one of Toronto's largest Reform congregations.

Temple Sinai began with an organising meeting at the Grosberg home in May 1954. That summer the fourteen founding families hired Jordan Pearlson, a 29-year-old rabbinical student from Hebrew Union College who had trained as an engineer and a lawyer before turning to the rabbinate, even before land had been bought or a building fund opened. Holy Blossom Temple lent the new congregation a Torah scroll and money to get started, and one of its first formal services was held in the nearby Asbury and West United Church, a gesture of goodwill from its pastor that set the tone for Rabbi Pearlson's lifelong interfaith work.

Building began only two years later, and the present synagogue at 210 Wilson Avenue was dedicated in October 1958 with 367 member families. Rabbi Pearlson served the congregation for about forty years, until the mid-1990s, and saw it grow to close to 1,800 families; he wrote a religion column for the Toronto Star and pioneered a daily interfaith dialogue on CBC Radio. He died on 19 February 2008 at 83. The chapel where the weekday morning minyan meets bears his name.

Temple Sinai today has more than 1,750 member households, making it one of the largest Reform congregations in Canada. It is led by Rabbi Michael Dolgin as senior rabbi with Rabbi Jordan Shaner, and has nurtured several rabbis of its own, among them Erin Polansky, who grew up in the congregation and later served as its associate rabbi. Its program ranges from Omer study and a daily minyan to bridge, canasta and photography groups, and it sees itself as a warm and welcoming Jewish community, not just a Reform synagogue.

A music-centred, fully egalitarian Reform congregation founded in 1971 by families who believed a temple could flourish northeast of Toronto.

Temple Har Zion was founded in 1971 by a few families who believed that a Reform temple could flourish northeast of Toronto, in what was then the edge of the suburbs. Their vision was of a temple as an extension of the home, a place where every member of a family would feel comfortable. The congregation's synagogue stands on Bayview Avenue in Thornhill.

Music is at the heart of worship at Har Zion. Its clergy, Rabbi Cory Weiss and Cantor Rachael Littman, have each composed liturgy for synagogues, and together they weave music through Shabbat services that are engaging and participatory. Rabbi Michael Stroh, who led the congregation for many years, is rabbi emeritus.

Fully egalitarian, Temple Har Zion holds daily morning services, weekly Torah study, a monthly family service and a monthly Tot Shabbat. Its religious school runs on Sunday mornings for junior kindergarten to Grade 6 and on Tuesday evenings for Grades 7 to 10, with Hebrew taught in a separate Beit Ivrit stream.

Founded in 1988 by families who dreamed of an inclusive synagogue built around Shabbat and learning, and housed since 2021 on the Vaughan Jewish Community Campus.

Temple Kol Ami, 'Voice of My People', began in 1988 when a small group of families dreamed of an inclusive synagogue centred on Shabbat and learning. The first services were held in members' homes and later at the Dufferin Clark Community Centre; the first High Holy Day services, for thirteen families, were held at Leo Baeck Day School's former home on Kenton Drive and led by Rabbi Steven Garten, then the school's director. After a summer service in a member's backyard in 1990, Rabbi Nancy Wechsler became the founding rabbi, and served until 1996.

Rabbi Daniel Gottlieb followed, then Rabbi Sharon Sobel as interim for six months, and from 2011 Rabbi Micah Streiffer. The congregation rented space for many years at Leo Baeck Day School in Thornhill. In 2001 it bought land at 8777 Dufferin Street, but never built there and sold it in 2010; plans to move to the Lebovic Jewish Community Campus and partner with Bialik Hebrew Day School also fell through. By its 25th anniversary in 2013 it had grown to about 170 families, and its leaders said that more than eighty per cent of members attended services or school or volunteered.

Kol Ami's religious school meets on Saturday mornings and Wednesday evenings; on Shabbat the children go upstairs to class while parents study Torah and pray, and the families come together at noon for a family education service. In 2018 the members of Neshamah Congregation of York Region were proposed to merge into Kol Ami. Since 2021 the congregation has been housed in the Kimel Family Education Centre on the Vaughan Jewish Community Campus on Bathurst Street.

A no-building, low-dues Reform congregation founded in 2011 for young families in Thornhill Woods; its members were proposed to join Temple Kol Ami in 2018.

Neshamah, Hebrew for 'soul', was founded in 2011 by Rabbi Erin Polansky as a Reform congregation for the young families of Thornhill Woods in Vaughan. Rabbi Polansky, who grew up in Thornhill and had served as associate rabbi at Temple Sinai in Toronto, built it on a deliberately light model: no building and low dues, with services and classes at the North Thornhill Community Centre and in members' homes. Its Judaism was open, accessible, non-judgmental and accepting, with a focus on community and on the Jewish education of children and adults.

By 2017 about 150 families belonged. In 2018 the members were proposed to merge into Temple Kol Ami, the established Reform congregation nearby, and Rabbi Polansky's service to Neshamah ended that year; she later became rabbi of Beth Israel Congregation in Kingston.
Neshamah's registered charity status was revoked by the Canada Revenue Agency on 4 December 2021 and its federal corporation was dissolved on 27 April 2024.

Niagara Falls' only synagogue, formed in 2000 by Canada's first Conservative-Reform merger; its 1937 Ferry Street building was sold in 2020.

Jews in Niagara Falls crossed the river to Niagara Falls, New York, for the holidays until about 1918, when there were enough of them to form a minyan of their own. In 1922 letters patent for the B'nai Yankev, or B'nai Jacob, Congregation were signed by Myer Salit, Louis Wertman, Sam Greenspan, Hyman Ornstein and Harry Kamisky, and Salit and Jacob Rosberg donated a Torah. The synagogue on Ferry Street, in the heart of the city's tourist centre, was built between 1934 and 1937 and stayed in continuous use from 1937. The community peaked in the 1960s at eighty to ninety families, and the building gained seven stained-glass windows by Ira Ginsburg.

Across the region in St. Catharines, Temple Tikvah had been established in 1972 as a Reform alternative to the Conservative B'nai Israel, a dozen families meeting in homes before renting a chapel at Mountainview United Church and, from 1974, space at St. George's Anglican Church downtown. In 1977 it became the first synagogue in Canada to hire a female rabbi, the 27-year-old student Vicky Hollander, who commuted from Cincinnati twice a month, and in 1992 it hired the second, Ellen Wierzba.

In January 2000 the two shrinking congregations amalgamated, the first time in Canada that a Conservative and a Reform congregation had joined together. The merged congregation, called B'nai Tikvah, worshipped in the former B'nai Jacob building with about sixty families and forty Hebrew-school students; Bob Muller and Chuck Shulman were co-presidents, and Muller, a local businessman, later served as spiritual director. That same year it donated a Torah scroll to the new congregation in Barrie. Services were held monthly, and the congregation held four Torah scrolls, one of them a Czech memorial scroll, one of only eleven that came to Canada.

After years of difficult discussion about maintaining an aging building with a dwindling membership, the Ferry Street synagogue was sold in November 2020 to a developer who planned to demolish it. The congregation arranged for six of the seven stained-glass windows and its memorial plaques to be placed in a Holocaust memorial in the Jewish section of a Niagara Falls cemetery, with the seventh window on loan to a local museum. The congregation closed soon after.

An aliyah (plural aliyot, 'going up') is being called to the Torah scroll to say the blessings before and after a section of the reading. You do not read the scroll yourself: in most congregations a designated reader (ba'al koreh) does that. Rehearse the steps below, then ask the person in charge (the gabbai, or the rabbi or cantor) how your congregation does each one.
Tell the gabbai (the person who organises who is called up) that you would like or are expected to have an aliyah, and which one if you know.
Have your Hebrew name ready, and your father's Hebrew name. Some congregations also use your mother's name; ask.
Ask which aliyah you have and whether the blessings are on a card at the reading table.
Ask what the dress custom is (head covering, tallit). Many synagogues lend one.
How should my Hebrew name be given?
Is there a card with the blessings?

The gabbai or the reader calls you in Hebrew by your Hebrew name and your father's name. In many congregations the call begins with the word Ya'amod ('let him stand'); the wording varies and may be different for a woman.
Stand and go up to the platform (bimah) where the scroll is read. The gabbai may meet you and show the way.
The scroll is open on the reading table. You stand at the table next to the reader. Which side of the reader you stand on is a custom that this app does not record.
Let the gabbai show you the exact spot.
Find the place and touch the scroll
Many people touch the scroll at the first word of the section with the corner of a tallit, a sash, or the scroll's cover, kiss what touched it, and hold the wooden handles (atzei chayim).
Do what the gabbai shows you. Do not touch the writing with a finger.
You call the congregation to bless. They answer.
You say the first line. The congregation answers with the second line.
In many congregations you then say the second line yourself too, before the blessing; watch what the person before you does.
You say the blessing. The congregation answers: Amen.
Say it clearly. If you stumble, keep going; the gabbai is beside you.
The reader chants the section from the scroll. Your part is to stand there and follow along.
Look at the text where the reader is. You do not read aloud.
At the end of the section
When the reader finishes, many people touch the scroll again near the last words and kiss it, as at the start, and hold the handles.
Do what the gabbai shows you.
You say the second blessing. The congregation answers: Amen.
Say it, then wait for the gabbai to tell you what happens next.

You may be offered a Mi sheberach, a prayer for you and your family, said by the gabbai or the reader. People often greet you with 'Yasher koach' ('more power to you'). Whether you stay at the table until the next person finishes, and where you sit afterwards, varies by congregation.
Ask the gabbai beforehand whether to stay at the table.

Cantillation (trope): not taught here, and why
Short explainer. No claim here is about a particular community's melodies. Not reviewed by a cantor.
In a printed Chumash (a book of the Torah), many words carry extra small marks above and below the letters, besides the vowel points. These are cantillation marks, called te'amim in Hebrew, or trope.
They show the melody motif for each word and also mark how phrases join and pause, so they work both as musical notation and as punctuation.
A Torah scroll has no vowel points and no cantillation marks. A reader has to know both the vowels and the tune for every word.
The texts in this app deliberately leave the cantillation marks out, so that you can see the letters and vowels clearly. (They were removed from the source texts when the corpus was built.)
The melodies are passed on by ear and differ between communities. This app has no recording by a qualified cantor, so teaching them from here would mean guessing.
You do not need trope to have an aliyah. The person called up says the blessings; in most congregations a designated reader chants the scroll.

'Which should I learn?' guide for an English-speaking learner in the US. Written to inform, not to rank traditions. The evidence on what American congregations actually do is thin: one published survey measured one or two words. Every entry says so and tells the learner to check their own congregation.

The only quantitative source read is Benor and Cohen's survey (BJPA). It asked which form of 'Festival of Booths' people use; 'soo-COAT' (Israeli) was chosen by 68% of Reform, 73% of Conservative, 70% of Modern Orthodox, 50% of Orthodox and 38% of Black Hat respondents, 'SUK-kiss' (Ashkenazic) by 34, 34, 47, 67 and 73% (people could pick both, so rows add to more than 100). Self-reported, snowball sample, not representative, one word. It tells you tendencies, not what your synagogue does.
Ask the people you will pray with. Listen to a service or a recording from your own congregation before you choose.
Practice varies inside a single synagogue: the cantor, the rabbi, older members and the Torah reader may each say things differently.
Chabad.org's own article says all dialects of Hebrew are acceptable; it is a matter of community custom, not of right and wrong.

If you are unsure, learn the Israeli-based sounds first. They are what the Hebrew of Israel uses and what most non-Orthodox respondents in the survey reported, and the Ashkenazi switches (tav, kamatz, cholam, tsere, stress) can be added afterwards.

Why does Israeli Hebrew sound Sephardi? A short story for beginners

Hebrew letters have been spelled the same way for two thousand years, but Jews in different countries said them differently. Jews in Spain, North Africa and the Middle East (Sephardim) kept one set of sounds; Jews in Germany and Eastern Europe (Ashkenazim) kept another. The famous test: the vowel kamatz is ah for Sephardim and o for Ashkenazim, so the same word is Shabbat for one and Shabbos for the other, and the letter tav without a dot is t for one and s for the other.

Around 1900, when people started speaking Hebrew every day again in the land of Israel, almost all of them had grown up with the Ashkenazi sounds. They chose the Sephardi sounds anyway. Why? The old Jewish community of Jerusalem was Sephardi and was respected; Eliezer Ben-Yehuda and the first Hebrew teachers worked with them; the Bible's own stress marks put the accent at the end of most words, which is how Sephardim read; and the new settlers wanted a sound that was not the sound of the European villages they had left behind.

In 1903 the Hebrew teachers' assembly in Palestine made it official: the new schools would teach the Sephardi pronunciation. Children learned it; their parents mostly did not. Writers who arrived later, such as the novelist Agnon, kept an Ashkenazi tinge all their lives, and old kibbutz members could still be heard stressing words the Ashkenazi way.

The new Israeli accent took the Sephardi vowels and stress, but it was spoken by European mouths. Two Sephardi sounds did not survive the move: the throaty ayin and the throaty chet. Most Israelis today say ayin as a silent letter and chet like the kh in khaf, and they say resh at the back of the throat, where Sephardim roll it at the front. That is why this app has three settings and not two: Modern Israeli is the Sephardi system without the throat sounds.

What this means for you: if you will read in a Reform or Conservative synagogue in North America, the Israeli-style sounds are what you will hear most, with a few Ashkenazi words kept by habit. If your community is Sephardi or Mizrahi, add the throat sounds for ayin and chet and roll the r. If it is Orthodox Ashkenazi, expect Shabbos, Borukh and oy-sounds. None of these is wrong; each is a community's way of reading the same letters.
